<C>APPENDIX</C>
<SHL>
<C>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</C>
<P><SC>The</SC> year in which Shakespeare first wrote <I>Hamlet</I> has given rise to much dis-
cussion.
<P>From fourteen to sixteen years before the date of the first edition that has come
down to us of this tragedy, allusions to a Play apparently bearing the same title, and
containing the same plot, are to be found in contemporary literature.
<P>The question that still divides the Shakespearian world is, stated broadly, whether
or not this older drama be one of Shakespeare's earliest works.
<P>The earliest allusion to it was pointed out by <SC>Dr Farmer</SC>, in his <I>Essay on the
Learning of Shakespeare</I> (ed. ii, p. 85). The allusion is contained in an Epistle
&lquo;To the Gentlemen Students of both Universities,&rquo; written by Nash, and prefixed to
Greene's <I>Menaphon,</I> or <I>Arcadia,</I> printed in 1589. Nash, referring to the makers of
plays of that day, says: Ile turne backe to my first text, of studies of delight, and
talke a little in friendship with a few of our triviall translators. It is a common
practice now a daies amongst a sort of shifting companions, that runne through every
arte and thrive by none to leave the trade of <I>Noverint</I> whereto they were borne, and
busie themselves with the indevours of art, that could scarcelie latinize their necke-
verse if they should have neede; yet English Seneca read by candle-light yeeldes
manie good sentences, as <I>Blould is a begger,</I> and so foorth: and if you intreate him
faire in a frostie morning, he will affoord you whole <I>Hamlets,</I> I should say Hand-
fulls of tragical speaches.<SUP>*</SUP> But O grief! <I>Tempus edax rerum;</I>&mdash;what is it that
will last always? The sea exhaled by drops will in continuance be drie; and Seneca,
let bloud line by line, and page by page, at length must needs die to our stage.&rquo;
<P><SC>Malone</SC> (<I>Variorum,</I> 1821, vol. ii, p. 372), after quoting this passage, continues:
Not having seen the first edition of this tract till a few years ago, I formerly doubted
whether the foregoing passage referred to the tragedy of <I>Hamlet;</I> but the word
<I>Hamlets</I> being printed in the original copy in a different character from the rest, I
have no longer any doubt upon the subject. It is manifest from this passage that
some play on the story of <I>Hamlet</I> had been exhibited before the year 1589; but I
am inclined to think that it was not Shakespeare's drama, but an elder performance,
on which, with the aid of the old prose <I>Hystorie of Hamblet,</I> his tragedy was formed.
The great number of pieces which we <I>know</I> he formed on the performances of pre-
ceding writers, renders it highly probable that some others also of his dramas were
<FHL>
<NOTE>* Thus far in this extract <*> have followed Staunton; the rest is as Malone quotes it. <SC>Ed.</SC></NOTE>
<PB N=6>
<HE>6 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>constructed on plays that are now lost. Perhaps the original <I>Hamlet</I> was written by
Thomas Kyd; who was the author of one play (and probably of more) to which no
name is affixed. The only tragedy to which Kyd's name is affixed (<I>Cornelia</I>) is a
professed <I>translation</I> from the French of Garnier, who, as well as his translator,
imitated Seneca. In Kyd's <I>Spanish Tragedy,</I> as in Shakespeare's <I>Hamlet,</I> there is,
if I may say so, a play represented <I>within a play;</I> if the old play of <I>Hamlet</I> should
ever be recovered, a similar interlude, I make no doubt, would be found there; and
somewhat of the same contrivance may be traced in the old <I>Taming of a Shrew,</I> a
comedy which perhaps had the same author as the other ancient pieces now enume-
rated. Nash seems to point at some dramatic writer of that time who had originally
been a scrivener or attorney, and instead of transcri<*> deeds and pleadings, had
chosen to imitate Seneca's plays, of which a translation had been published many
years before. Shakespeare, however freely he may have borrowed from Plutarch or
Holinshed, does not appear to be at all indebted to Seneca; and therefore I do not
believe that he was the person in Nash's contemplation.&rquo; Malone was inclined to
believe at first that the person alluded to as having left the trade of <I>Noverint</I> (that
is, of attorney, from the Latin formula with which deeds began; <I>Noverint Universi,</I>
and of which our <I>Know all men</I> is a translation) could not have been Shakespeare;
but afterwards, on a review of the numerous legal terms and phrases used by Shake-
speare, he changed his opinion, and suspected that Shakespeare &lquo;was early initiated
in at least the forms of law; and was employed, while at Stratford, in the office of
some country attorney who was at the same time a petty conveyancer, and perhaps
also the Seneschal of some manor-court.&rquo;
<P>In reference to the date of this <I>Epistle</I> of Nash's, <SC>Dyce</SC> in his edition of Greene's
<I>Works</I> (vol. i, p. ciii), after citing the title of <I>Menaphon. Camillas alarum to slum-
bering Euphues, in his melancholie Cell at Silexedra.</I> &amp;c., &amp;c., 1589, 4to, adds:
&lquo;First printed 1587,&rquo; but gives no authority in the way of title or imprint. This date of
1587 has been followed, on Dyce's authority, by Collier and one or two others, but
<SC>Knight</SC> thinks it is a mistake, and Dyce himself seems to have had a misgiving on
the subject, for in his second edition of Shakespeare he gives the date of Greene's
<I>Menaphon</I> as 1589 with &lquo;[qy if first printed in 1587?]&rquo; after it. The surer date,
therefore, is 1589. This date is of importance; it makes Shakespeare twenty-five
years old, instead of twenty-three, when Nash thus alluded to him,&mdash;no small gain
for those who maintain that this older <I>Hamlet</I> was written by him.
<P><SC>C. A. Brown</SC> (<I>Shakespeare's Autobiographical Poems,</I> p. 254) maintains emphat-
ically that Shakespeare's tragedy was referred to in the phrase &lquo;whole <I>Hamlets</I> of
tragical speaches,&rquo; and that Shakespeare himself was alluded to as having left the
trade of <I>Noverint;</I> and further, that his reason for assigning 1589 as the date of the
composition of <I>Hamlet</I> is &lquo;founded solely on this passage from Nash. It is to be
understood as regarding its original state before the alterations and enlargements had
taken place.&rquo; . . . &lquo;If there exists a description of that elder play, I do not hesi-
tate in saying it is Shakespeare's and no other's, provided the Ghost appears in it.
According to the old black-letter Quarto, whence the tragedy is derived, the killing
of the Prince's father was public; consequently, no Ghost was employed to reveal
it to the son. Now the change from an open slaying, with some show of cause, to a
secret murder, involving the necessity of the Ghost's appearance to seek revenge, is
so important, so wonderful an invention for the dramatic effect of the story, that I
cannot imagine it belonged to any but Shakespeare. Should I be mistaken in this
opinion, still I appeal to Nash's authority, published in 1589, that Shakespeare's
<PB N=7>
<HE><I>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</I> 7</HE>
<P><I>Hamlet</I> had been played: the word in Italics, &ldquo;<I>Hamlets,</I>&rdquo; proving that <I>Hamlet</I> was
then on the stage, and that it had been written by a &ldquo;Noverint,&rdquo; or lawyer's clerk;
while the examples which I have given of Shakespeare's law-phrases, and which
might be multiplied tenfold at least, if sought in all his works, prove that such must
have been the employment of his early days.&rquo;
<P><SC>Knight</SC> agrees with Brown, and sees nothing, on the score of Shakespeare's
youth, &lquo;extravagant in his [Brown's] belief,&rquo; adding: &lquo;Let it be remembered that
in that very year [1589], when Shakespeare was twenty-five, it has been distinctly
proved by Collier that he was a sharer in the Blackfriars theatre with others, and
some of note, below him in the list of sharers.&rquo;
<P>In reference to this <I>Epistle</I> of Nash's, <SC>Staunton</SC> says: &lquo;Here the &ldquo;shifting com-
panions, that runne through every arte,&rdquo; brings so distinctly to mind the epithet &ldquo;an
absolute <I>Johannes Factotum,</I>&rdquo; which Nash's sworn brother, Greene, in his <I>Groats-
worth of Wit,</I> &amp;c., 1593, applied to Shakespeare; and &ldquo;the trade of <I>Noverint</I>&rdquo; so
well tallies with the received tradition of his having passed some time in the office
of an attorney, that, <I>prim&acirc; facie,</I> the allusion to <I>Hamlet</I> would seem directly levelled
at our author's tragedy. But then interposes a difficulty on the score of dates.
Shakespeare, in 1589, was only twenty-three [<I>sic</I>] years old,&mdash;too young, it may be
well objected, to have earned the distinction of being satirized by Nash as having
&ldquo;run through every art.&rdquo; It is asserted, too, on good authority that an edition
of the <I>Menaphon</I> was published in 1587, and if that earlier copy contained Nash's
<I>Epistle,</I> the probability of his referring to Shakespeare is considerably weakened.&rquo;
<P>Just as Malone's edition of 1790 was issuing from the press, there was found at
Dulwich College a large Folio MS volume, containing valuable information respect-
ing theatrical affairs from the year 1591 to 1609. The volume is in the handwriting
of Philip Henslowe, a proprietor, or joint lessee, of more than one theatre during
that period, and contains, among others, his accounts of receipts and expenditures
in connection with his theatrical management. Malone reprinted copious extracts
from this MS in the first volume of his edition; but it was reprinted entire by the
&lquo;Shakespeare Society&rquo; in 1845, with a valuable Preface by Collier, from which the
following extracts are given, which, although not strictly germane to the First Quarto
of <I>Hamlet,</I> contain much important aid in estimating the value of the theories re-
specting it. But, first, a few words as to the <I>Diary</I> itself: &lquo;Henslowe,&rquo; says Collier,
&lquo;was an ignorant man, even for the time in which he lived, and for the station he oc-
cupied; he wrote a bad hand, adopted any orthography that suited his notions of the
sound of words, especially of proper names (necessarily of most frequent occurrence),
and he kept his book, as respects dates in particular, in the most disorderly, negligent,
and confused manner. Sometimes, indeed, he observes a sort of system in his entries;
but often, when he wished to make a note, he seems to have opened his book at
random, and to have written what he wanted in any space he found vacant. He
generally used his own pen, but, as we have stated, in some places the hand of a
scribe or clerk is visible; and here and there the dramatists and actors themselves
wrote the item in which they were concerned, for the sake, perhaps, of saving the
old manager trouble; thus, in various parts of the manuscript, we meet with the
handwriting, not merely the signatures, of Drayton, Chapman, Dekker, Chettle,
Porter, Wilson, Hathaway, Day, S. Rowley, Haughton, Rankins, and Wadeson;
but, although frequently mentioned, we have no specimen of the handwriting of
Nash, Ben Jonson, Middleton, Webster, Marston, or Heywood.&rquo; Where the names
<PB N=8>
<HE>8 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>of nearly all dramatic poets of the age are to be frequently found, we might certainly
count on finding that of Shakespeare, but the shadow within which Shakespeare's
earthly life was spent envelops him here, too, and &lquo;his name,&rquo; as <SC>Collier</SC> says, &lquo;is
not met with in any part of the manuscript.&rquo; &lquo;At various times and for uncertain
periods, Henslowe was more or less interested in the receipts obtained by players
acting under the names of the Queen, Lord Nottingham, Lord Strange, Lord Sussex,
Lord Worcester, and the Lord Chamberlain. The latter was the company of which
Shakespeare was a member, either as actor or author, from his first arrival in, until
his final retirement from, London; which company, after the accession of James I.
was allowed to assume the distinguishing title of <I>The King's Players.</I>&rquo;
<P>So much for the general character of this interesting volume; the portion of the
contents that is most important is the period which it covers from 3 June, 1594, to
18 July, 1596; during the whole of this time the <I>Lord Admiral's Players</I> were
jointly occupying, or possibly playing in combination at, the theatre at Newington
Butts with the <I>Lord Chamberlain's Players;</I> &lquo;and here we find by Henslowe that
no fewer than forty new plays were got up and acted. For about ten days of the
two years the companies ceased to perform, on account, perhaps, of the heat of the
weather, and the occurrence of Lent; so that two years are the utmost upon which a
calculation can be made, and the result of it is, that the audiences of that day re-
quired a new play upon an average about every eighteen days, including Sundays.
The rapidity with which plays must then have been written is most remarkable, and
is testified beyond dispute by later portions of Henslowe's manuscript, where, among
other charges, he registers the sums paid, the dates of payment, and the authors who
received the money. Nothing was more common than for dramatists to unite their
abilities and resources, and when a piece on any account was to be brought out with
peculiar dispatch, three, four, five, and perhaps even six poets engaged themselves
on different portions of it. Evidence of this dramatic combination will be found
of such frequent occurrence that it is vain here to point out particular pages where
it is to be met with.&rquo; The union of the two companies of players just referred to
lasted a little more than two years. Possibly it may have been merely a joint occu-
pation of the same theatre while the Globe was building, but at any rate it is singular
that while it lasted, whatever may have been its character, &lquo;most of the old plays
which our great dramatist is supposed, more or less, to have employed, and of the
stories of which he availed himself, are found in Henslowe's list of this period.
Here we find a <I>Titus Andronicus,</I> a <I>Lear,</I> a <I>Hamlet,</I> a <I>Henry V,</I> and a <I>Henry VI,</I>
a Buckingham, the old <I>Taming of a Shrew,</I> and several others. For aught we
know, Shakespeare may have had originally some share in their authorship, or if he
had not, as he probably acted in them, he may have felt himself authorised, as a
member of the company, to use them to the extent that answered his purpose. . . . .
No fact is more clearly made out, and very much by the evidence Henslowe fur-
nishes, than that it was a very common practice for our early dramatists to avail
themselves of the materials, whether of plot, character, or language, supplied by
their immediate predecessors, and even by their actual contemporaries.&rquo;
<P>Five lines before the entry in Henslowe's diary there is this memorandum: &lquo;In
the name of God Amen, beginninge at Newington, my Lord Admeralle and my
Lorde chamberlen men, as foloweth. 1594.&rquo; (It is to be borne in mind that Shake-
speare was one of the &lquo;Lorde chamberlen men&rquo; at this date.&rquo;)
<P>The entry itself is as follows:
<BQ>
9 of June 1594, Rd at hamlet . . . . viijs<LB>
</BQ>
<PB N=9>
<HE><I>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</I> 9</HE>
<P>In a note <SC>Malone</SC> says: &lquo;In the <I>Essay on the Order of Shakespeare's Plays,</I> I
have stated my opinion [quoted above], that there was a play on the subject of
<I>Hamlet</I> prior to our author's, and here we have a full confirmation of that conjec-
ture. It cannot be supposed that our poet's play should have been performed but
once in the time of this account, and that Henslowe should have drawn from such
a piece but the sum of eight shillings, when his share in several other plays came to
three and sometimes four pounds. It is clear that not one of our author's plays was
played at Newington Butts; if one had been performed, we should certainly have
found more.&rquo;
<P><SC>Collier's</SC> note (p. 35, ed. <I>Sh. Soc.</I>) is as follows: &lquo;Malone contends, we think
correctly, that this was the old <I>Hamlet,</I> and not Shakespeare's play. [If this be
the case], our great dramatist might adopt the story, and feel that he had a better
right to do so, because the old play had been acted by his friends and fellows, or
perhaps with their assistance.&rquo;
<P>Among other peculiarities of Henslowe's diary is the custom which he adopted
of marking each <I>new</I> play with the abbreviation <I>ne.</I> The above entry has no such
mark; it is therefore to be inferred that it was not a first performance.
<P>The next trace that we find of the old tragedy is in Lodge's <I>Wits miserie,</I> which
also was discovered by Dr <SC>Farmer</SC> (<I>Essay,</I> &amp;c., p. 75, second edition, 1767), who,
however, supposed that the allusion by Lodge referred to Shakespeare's own play,
and not to any older tragedy. Aubrey having said that Shakespeare &lquo;did act <I>exceed-
ingly well,</I>&rquo; Farmer denies that we have any reason to suppose so, because &lquo;Rowe
tells us from the information of Betterton, who was inquisitive into this point, and
had very early opportunities of inquiry from Sir W. Davenant, that he was no <I>extra-
ordinary actor,</I> and that the top of his performance was the Ghost in his own
<I>Hamlet.</I> Yet this <I>chef d'&oelig;uvre</I> did not please; I will give you an original stroke
at it. Dr Lodge, who was for ever pestering the town with pamphlets, published in
the year 1596, <I>Wits miserie, and the Worlds madnesse, discovering the Devils incar-
nat of this Age.</I> One of these Devils is <I>Hate-Virtue,</I> or <I>Sorrow for another mans
good Success,</I> who, says the Doctor, is &ldquo;<I>a foule lubber,</I> and looks as pale as the
visard of y<SUP>e</SUP> ghost, which cried so miserally [<I>sic</I>] at y<SUP>e</SUP> theator, like an oisterwife,
<I>Hamlet reuenge.</I>&rdquo; &rquo;
<P>This phrase, &lquo;Hamlet, revenge!&rquo; made a deep impression on the popular mind,
and is referred to more than once before the present <I>Hamlet</I> appeared and obliterated
the memory of it.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (<I>Preliminary Note to Hamlet,</I> p. 100): My own conviction is . . . . that
the piece alluded to by Nash and Lodge, and acted at Newington, was an earlier
tragedy on the same subject, which no longer exists, and which probably (like many
other old dramas) never reached the press.
<P><SC>Staunton</SC> remarks: &lquo;After duly weighing the evidence on either side, we incline
to agree with Dyce, that the play alluded to by Lodge and Nash was an earlier pro-
duction on the same subject; though we find no cause to conclude that the first
sketch of Shakespeare's <I>Hamlet,</I> as published in 1603, was not the piece to which
Henslowe refers in his entry, connected with the performance at Newington Butts.&rquo;
<P>In the <I>Variorum</I> of 1773, <SC>Steevens</SC> says: &lquo;I have hitherto met with no earlie$
edition of this play [<I>Hamlet</I>] than the one in the year 1605 [1604,&mdash;<I>Var.</I> 1778], tho'
it must have been performed before that time, as I have seen a copy of Speght's
<PB N=10>
<HE>10 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>edition of Chaucer, which formerly belonged to Dr Gabriel Harvey (the antagonist
of Nash), who, in his own handwriting, has set down the play as a performance
with which he was well acquainted, in the year 1598. His words are these: &ldquo;The
younger sort take much delight in Shakespeare's <I>Venus and Adonis,</I> but his <I>Lucre<*></I>
and his tragedy of <I>Hamlet Prince of Denmarke,</I> have it in them to please the wiser
sort, 1598.&rdquo; &rquo;
<P>In consequence of this note of Steevens, <SC>Malone</SC> was induced to believe that
Shakespeare's <I>Hamlet</I> was first published in 1596, but afterwards, in the <I>Variorum</I>
of 1821 (ii, 369), he has the following note: &lquo;In a former edition of this <I>Essay,</I>
I was induced to suppose that <I>Hamlet</I> must have been written prior to 1598, from
the loose manner in which Mr Steevens has mentioned a manuscript note by Ga-
briel Harvey, in a copy, which had belonged to him, of Speght's <I>Chaucer,</I> in which,
we are told, he has set down <I>Hamlet</I> as a performance with which he was well ac-
quainted in 1598. But I have been favored by the Bishop of Dromore [Dr Percy],
the possessor of the book referred to, with an inspection of it, and, on an attentive
examination, I have found reason to believe that the note in question may have been
written in the latter end of the year 1600. Harvey doubtless purchased this volume
in 1598, having, both at the beginning and end of it, written his name. But it by no
means follows that all the intermediate remarks which are scattered throughout were
put down at the same time. He speaks of <I>translated Tasso</I> in one passage; and
the first edition of Fairfax, which is doubtless alluded to, appeared in 1600.&rquo;
<P>Wherefore, and in consequence of the allusion to the &lquo;inhibition&rquo; of the players
spoken of in <I>Hamlet,</I> II, ii, 320, Malone supposed <I>Hamlet</I> to have appeared first in
1600.
<P>According to <SC>Singer</SC> (<I>Preliminary Remarks to Hamlet,</I> p. 152, 1826), the <I>trans-
lated Tasso,</I> referred to by Malone, need not necessarily have been Fairfax's trans-
lation of 1600, but Harvey may have alluded to the version of the first five books
of the <I>Jerusalem,</I> published by R. C[arew] in 1594. Singer therefore &lquo;safely
places the date of the first composition of <I>Hamlet</I> at least as early as 1597.&rquo;
<P><SC>Knight</SC>: Not a tittle of distinct evidence exists to show that there was any other
play of <I>Hamlet</I> but that of Shakespere; and all the collateral evidence upon
which it is inferred that an earlier play of <I>Hamlet</I> than Shakspere's did exist may,
on the other hand, be taken to prove that Shakspere's original sketch of <I>Hamlet</I>
was in repute at an earlier period than is commonly assigned to its date. . . . . In
Henslowe's diary, the very next entry is &lquo;at the taminge of a shrewe;&rquo; and Malone,
in a note, adds: &lquo;the play which preceded Shakespeare's.&rquo; When Malone wrote
this note he believed that Shakspere's <I>Taming of the Shrew</I> was a late production;
but in the second edition of his &lquo;Chronological Order&rquo; he is persuaded that it was
one of his <I>very early</I> productions. &lquo;There is nothing,&rquo; says Knight in conclusion,
&lquo;to prove that <I>both</I> these plays thus acted were not Shakspere's.&rquo;
<P><SC>Malone</SC>, in his edition of 1790, finds another reference to this old traged in
Jonson's <I>The Case is Altered,</I> which was written before the end of 1599. It is as
follows: &lquo;But first I'll play the ghost; I'll call him out.&rquo; The allusion is so very
doubtful that Malone did not refer to it in his subsequent editions. As Gifford says,
we might as well find an allusion in &lquo;the ghost of every play that has appeared since
the days of Thespis.&rquo;
<P>The last allusion to this old tragedy that we find before the publication of the
First Quarto in 1603 is given by <SC>Capell</SC> (<I>Notes,</I> iii, 232), and bears witness to the

<P>distinguishing phrase before quoted: &lquo;<I>Asinius.</I> Wod I were hang'd if I can call

<P>This allusion by Dekker may be compared, says <SC>Halliwell</SC>, with another pas-

in the later Hamlet?].
<P><SC>Douce</SC> (ii, 265): In a poem, written by Anthony Scoloker, a printer, entitled

Faith it should please all, like Prince <I>Hamlet.</I> But in sadnesse, then it were to be
feared he would runne mad.&rquo;

<P>In <I>Eastward Hoe,</I> by Chapman, Jonson, and Marston, 1605, says <SC>Steevens</SC>, there
is a fling at the hero of this tragedy. A footman named Hamlet enters, and a
tankard-bearer asks him: &lquo;'Sfoote, Hamlet, are you mad?&rquo; <SC>Malone</SC> says there was
no satire intended. <I>Eastward Hoe</I> was acted at Shakespeare's own play-house (the
Blackfriars), by the &lquo;children of the revels.&rquo;
<P><SC>Steevens</SC> also cites from Dekker's <I>Bel-man's Night-walkes,</I> 1612:&mdash;&lquo;But if any
mad Hamlet, hearing this, smell villainie, and rush in hy violence,&rquo; &amp;c.
<P><SC>Dr Latham</SC> (<I>Two Dissertations on Hamlet,</I> &amp;c. London, 1872, p. 87) says that
we &lquo;know the date&rquo; of this older <I>Hamlet</I> to be 1589, but gives no proofs for his
assertion, and in the next sentence weakens our faith in his figures by stating that
Shakespeare was then in his twenty-third year. We are still more puzzled by
finding on page 91 a reference to the <I>Hamlet</I> of 1598. Under either date, I believe,
Dr Latham denies that this older <I>Hamlet,</I> referred to by Nash, Lodge, and others,
was written by Shakespeare, but maintains that &lquo;it is wholly or partially preserved&rquo;
in the text of the <I>Bestrafte Brudermord.</I> See Note prefixed to a translation of this
old German drama in this volume.
<P>The foregoing are all the allusions, I believe, to a play of <I>Hamlet</I> which many
critics believe preceded Shakespeare's tragedy. Some of these allusions that occur
after 1602 probably refer to Shakespeare's tragedy, but I have given them all be-
cause they are mentioned by one or another of the editors, and because it is proper
that in an edition for students, like this, every item of evidence should be set
forth.
<P>We now come to something more definitely connected with Shakespeare than
anything thus far.
<P><SC>Steevens</SC> discovered the following entry in the <I>Stationers' Registers:</I>

<P>(I have exactly followed the transcript of the entry as given by <SC>Arber</SC>.) Whether
or not the book, thus licensed, was printed in this year we cannot tell; no copy of it
has survived. That it was Shakespeare's tragedy we can have but little doubt, since
it was acted by the company to which he belonged. In the following spring, in 1603,
&lquo;The Lord Chamberlain's Servants&rquo; became &lquo;The King's Players,&rquo; and the Quarto pub-
lished in that year states that it had been acted &lquo;by his Highness' servants.&rquo; &lquo;Thus we
see,&rquo; says <SC>Collier</SC>, &lquo;that in July, 1602, there was an intention to print and publish a
play called <I>The Revenge of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke,</I> and this intention, we may
fairly conclude, arose out of the popularity of the piece, as it was then acted by &ldquo;the
Lord Chamberlain's Servants,&rdquo; who, in May following, obtained the title of &ldquo;the
King's Players.&rdquo; The object of Roberts, in making the entry, was to secure it to
himself, being, no doubt, aware that other printers and booksellers would endeavor
to anticipate him. It seems probable that he was unable to obtain such a copy of
<I>Hamlet</I> as he would put his name to; but some inferior and nameless printer, who
was not so scrupulous, having surreptitiously secured a manuscript of the play, how-
ever imperfect, which would answer the purpose, and gratify public curiosity, the
edition bearing date 1603 was published.&rquo;
<P>This edition of 1603 is reprinted in this volume; reference to the title-page will
show that although it is there stated to have been printed &lquo;at London&rquo; &lquo;for N. L.
[<I>i. e.</I> Nicholas Ling] and John Trundell,&rquo; no printer's name is mentioned. Hence
<SC>Collier's</SC> inference that the &lquo;nameless printer&rquo; was some unscrupulous rival of
James Robertes. But <SC>Dyce</SC> says (<I>Introduction to Hamlet,</I> p. 100, 1866), &lquo;we have no
proof that Roberts was not the &ldquo;nameless printer&rdquo; of the Quarto of 1603; on the con-
trary, there is reason to suspect that he was, since we find that he printed the next Quarto
of 1604 for the same Nicholas Ling, who was one of the publishers of the Quarto
of 1603.&rquo; The title-page of the Quarto published in 1604 states that it was printed
by J.[ames] R.[obertes] for N.[icholas] L.[ing]; wherefore Dyce's inference is
probably correct that James Roberts was also &lquo;the printer of the Quarto of 1603,
or what we now call the First Quarto.&rquo; <SC>Collier</SC>, in his second edition, in support
of his conjecture that Robertes did not print Q<SUB>1</SUB>, calls attention to the fact that Q<SUB>1</SUB>
&lquo;has Ling's device on the title-page, and that it was possibly from his types; the
edition of 1604 was printed for, not by, him;&rquo; be that as it may, it is a matter of
very small moment, and one thing is certain: that the edition, by whomsoever
printed, reflects but little credit on the printer; it gives a very inadequate idea of
the tragedy as it was acted, if not at the very time, certainly within a few months
afterwards. Possibly, if Roberts was the printer, this consciousness withheld his
name from the title-page of a publication whose chief object appears to have been to
forestall the market until something better could be furnished.
<P>It will be noticed, by referring to the Reprint p. 37, that on the title-page of
the Quarto of 1603 it is stated that it had been acted &lquo;in the two Vniuersities of
Cambridge and Oxford.&rquo; &lquo;No evidence,&rquo; says <SC>Clarendon</SC>, &lquo;has yet been discov-
ered of the occasion on which the play was acted at the two universities; but if we
might hazard a conjecture, it seems not improbable that it might have been at some
<PB N=13>
<HE><I>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</I> 13</HE>
<P>entertainment in honor of the king's accession, and it may have been selected as
being connected with the native country of his queen.&rquo;
<P>Of this edition of 1603 only two copies have survived, and both are imper-
fect; one lacks the title-page, and the other the last leaf. The Quarto of 1604 was
the earliest copy known down to 1823, when a copy of the Quarto of 1603 was
found by Sir Henry Bunbury, who gives the following account of it in his <I>Corre-
spondence of Sir Thomas Hanmer,</I> London, 1838, p. 80:&mdash;&lquo;[The only copy of the
First Quarto] known to be in existence, was found by me in a closet at Barton, 1823.
This curiosity (for a great curiosity it is, independently of its being an unique copy)
is now in the possession of the Duke of Devonshire; it probably was picked up by
my grandfather, Sir William Bunbury, who was an ardent collector of old dramas.
For the satisfaction of bibliographers, I take this opportunity of recording the par-
ticulars of the little volume, which contained this <I>Hamlet</I> of 1603. It was a small
quarto, barbarously cropped, and very ill-bound; its contents were as follows:&mdash;
<I>Merchant of Venice,</I> 1600, complete; <I>Merry Wives of Windsor,</I> 1602, do.; <I>Much
Ado about Nothing,</I> 1600, do.; <I>Midsummer Night's Dream,</I> 1600, do.; <I>Troilus
and Cressida</I> (wanting the title-page); <I>Romeo and Juliet,</I> 1599, complete; <I>Hamlet,</I>
1603 (wanting the last page); <I>Second Part of Henry the Fourth,</I> 1600, complete;
<I>First Part</I> of do., 1598, do.; <I>Henry the Fifth,</I> 1602, do.; <I>Richard the Third,</I> 1602,
do.; <I>Two Noble Kinsmen,</I> 1634, with MS corrections of the text. I exchanged the
volume with Messrs Payne and Foss, for books to the value of &pound;180, and they sold
it for &pound;230 to the Duke of Devonshire.&rquo;
<P>See also <I>The Athen&aelig;um,</I> 18 Oct. 1856, for a fuller account of this volume.
There was a reprint of this copy made by Payne and Foss in 1825, which is said
to be exceedingly accurate. It was lithographed in facsimile in 1858, under the
supervision of <SC>Collier</SC>, at the expense of the Duke of Devonshire. It was again
reprinted in 1860 under the supervision of <SC>S. Timmins</SC>, esq., with the Quarto of
1604 printed on opposite pages, &mdash;a highly valuable edition. It takes its place also
among the lithographic reprints by <SC>E. W. Ashbee</SC>, under the supervision of <SC>Halli-
well</SC>, and it is from this edition that the present reprint, in this volume, is made. It
is also reprinted with extreme accuracy in the Cambridge Edition.
<P>The <SC>Cambridge Editors</SC> state (I think without sufficient authority) that this copy
&lquo;belonged to Sir Thomas Hanmer, though he does not appear to have mentioned it
in his notes to Shakespeare, or in his correspondence, and its existence was not
known till his library came into the possession of Sir E. H. [<I>sic</I>] Bunbury in 1821.&rquo;
Sir H. E. Bunbury, as we have seen, believed that its original owner was his grand-
father, who was the nephew of Sir Thomas Hanmer.
<P>In 1856 the second copy, lacking the title-page, was bought from a student of
Trinity College, Dublin, by a Dublin book-dealer, for one shilling, and sold by him
for &pound;70; it was afterwards bought by Mr Halliwell for &pound;120, and is now in the
British Museum.
<P>The next year after the First Quarto was issued the Second Quarto was published,
with the following title-page:

was, according to the true and perfect &verbar; Coppie. &verbar; AT LONDON, &verbar; Printed by
I. R. for N. L. and are to be $old at his &verbar; $hoppe vnder Saint Dun$tons Church
in &verbar; Fleet$treet. 1604.

<P>Lowndes mentions an edition of 1604 as &lquo;printed by J. R. for N. Landure,&rquo; but
this is probably a mistake, which is repeated, however, in Halliwell's <I>Shakespeariana.</I>
It has found its way into several editions,&mdash;Knight's, for instance, as well as Elze's
and Francois Victor Hugo's. <SC>Elze</SC> called attention to it in <I>The Athen&aelig;um,</I> 11 Feb.
1860, and gave as his authority Halliwell's <I>Shakespeariana.</I> <SC>Halliwell</SC> replied
in the same Journal, 25 Feb. 1860: &lquo;I fear I have fallen into a blunder respect-
ing the name of the publisher of the <I>Hamlet</I> of 1604. The initials are all that are
given in the imprint, but the <I>fish</I> in the printer's device over the letters N. L. would
seem clearly to show that <I>Ling,</I> not Landure, was the publisher.&rquo;
<P>The statement that this edition is &lquo;enlarged to almost as much again as it was&rquo; is
correct enough for a bookseller's announcement,&mdash;there are about five hundred and
sixty-seven lines lacking to make it exactly as much again. The First Quarto num-
bers two thousand one hundred and forty-three lines; the Second Quarto about three
thousand seven hundred and nineteen.
<P>This notable difference in quantity, coupled with a marked difference in words,
phrases, and even in the order of the Scenes, together with a change in the names of
some of the characters, has given rise to an interesting discussion, which probably
will never be decided: it is whether, in the Quarto of 1603, we have the first draught
of Shakespeare's tragedy, which the author afterwards remodelled and elaborated
until it appears as we now have it substantially, in the Quarto of 1604, or is the First
Quarto merely a maimed and distorted version &lquo;of the true and perfect coppie&rquo;?
<P><SC>Collier</SC> was, I think, the first to maintain, from a careful comparison of the two,
that the copy of 1603 was printed from manuscript taken down in short-hand from
the players' mouths. <SC>Singer</SC> in his earlier edition in 1826, and in his later in 1856,
suggests that it may have been &lquo;printed from an imperfect manuscript of the prompt
books, or the play-house copy, or stolen from the author's papers. It is next to im-
possible that it can have been taken down during the representation. . . . . The
variations . . . . are too numerous and striking to admit of a doubt of the play
having been subsequently revised, amplified, and altered by the poet.&rquo;
<P><SC>Caldecott</SC> (<I>Preface to Hamlet,</I> 1832, p. vi): [This First Quarto exhibits] in that
which was afterwards wrought into a splendid drama, the first conception, and com-
paratively feeble expression of a great mind.
<P>The next and the chiefest advocate of this view is <SC>Knight</SC>, and his arguments are
here given almost in full; his extracts from Q<SUB>1</SUB> are omitted, and references to the
lines of the Reprint in this edition are substituted. His remarks are to be found in
the <I>Introductory Notice to Hamlet</I> in his edition of Shakespeare's Plays, p. 87; no
difference has been observed between his first and last editions, twenty-four years
apart.
<P>In the reprint of the edition of 1603 [by Payne and Foss, 1825], it is stated to
be the &lquo;only known copy of this tragedy <I>as originally written by Shakespeare,</I>
which he afterwards altered and enlarged.&rquo; We believe that this description is
correct; that this remarkable copy gives us the play as originally written by Shake-
speare. It may have been piratical, and we think it was so. It may, as Mr Collier
says, have been &lquo;published in haste from a short-hand copy taken from the mouths
of the players.&rquo; But this process was not applied to the present <I>Hamlet;</I> the
<I>Hamlet</I> of 1603 is a sketch of the perfect <I>Hamlet,</I> and probably a corrupt copy of
that sketch. We agree with Caldecott, and we think, further, that this first con-
ception was an early conception; that it was remodelled,&mdash;&lquo;enlarged to almost
as much againe as it was,&rquo;&mdash;at the beginning of the seventeenth century; and that
<PB N=15>
<HE><I>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</I> 15</HE>
<P>this original copy being then of comparatively little value was piratically pub-
lished. . . . . The highest interest of this edition consists, as we believe, in the
opportunity which it affords of studying the growth, not only of the great poet's
command over language,&mdash;not only of his dramatic skill,&mdash;but of the higher quali-
ties of his intellect,&mdash;his profound philosophy, his wonderful penetration into what
is most hidden and obscure in men's characters and motives. We request the
reader's indulgence whilst we attempt to point out some of the more important con-
siderations which have suggested themselves to us, in a careful study of this
original edition.
<P>And, first, let us state that all the <I>action</I> of the amended <I>Hamlet</I> is to be found in
the first sketch. The play opens with the Scene in which the Ghost appears to
Horatio and Marcellus. The order of the dialogue is the same; but, in the Quarto
of 1604, it is a little elaborated. The grand passage beginning: &lquo;In the most high
and palmy state of Rome,&rquo; is not found in this copy; and it is omitted in the Folio.
The Second Scene introduces us, as at present, to the King, Queen, Hamlet, Polo-
nius, and Laertes, but in this copy Polonius is called Corambis. The dialogue here
is much extended in the perfect copy. We will give an example. [Compare lines
173-179 of Q<SUB>1</SUB> with I, ii, 77-86.]
<P>We would ask if it is possible that such a careful working up of the first idea
could have been any other work than that of the poet himself? Can the alterations
be accounted for upon the principle that the first edition was an imperfect copy of
the complete play, &lquo;published in haste from a short-hand copy taken from the mouths
of the players? Could the players have transformed the line, &lquo;But I have that
within which passeth show,&rquo; into &lquo;Him have I lost, I must of force forego.&rquo; The
haste of short-hand does not account for what is truly the refinement of the poetical
art. The same nice elaboration is to be found in Hamlet's soliloquy in the same
scene. In the first copy we have not the passage so characteristic of Hamlet's
mind: &lquo;How weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable seem to me all the uses of this
world.&rquo; Neither have we the noble comparison of &lquo;Hyperion to a satyr.&rquo; The fine
Shaksperian phrase, so deep in its metaphysical truth, &lquo;a beast <I>that wants discourse
of reason,</I>&rquo; is in the first copy, &lquo;a beast <I>devoid of reason.</I>&rquo; Shakspere must have
dropt verse from his mouth, as the fairy in the Arabian tales dropt pearls. It appears
to have been no effort to him to have changed the whole arrangement of a poetical
sentence, and to have inverted its different members; he did this as readily as if he
were dealing with prose. In the first copy we have, &lquo;as if increase Of appetite had
grown by what it look'd on.&rquo; In the amended copy we have, &lquo;by what it fed on.&rquo;
Such changes are not the work of short-hand writers.
<P>The interview of Horatio, Bernardo, and Marcellus with Hamlet succeeds as in
the perfect copy, and the change here is very slight. The scene between Laertes
and Ophelia in the same manner follows. Here again there is a great extension.
The injunction of Laertes in the first copy is contained in these few lines. [See
lines 331-339 of Q<SUB>1</SUB>.]
<P>Compare this with the splendid passage which we now have. Look especially at
the four lines beginning, &lquo;For nature, crescent,&rquo; &amp;c. [I, iii, 11-14], in which we see
the deep philosophic spirit of the mature Shakspere. Polonius and his few precepts
next occur; and here again there is a slight difference. The lecture of the old
courtier to his daughter is somewhat extended. . . . .
<P>The character of Hamlet is fully conceived in the original play, whenever he is
in action, as in this scene [where Hamlet encounters the Ghost]. It is the contem-
<PB N=16>
<HE>16 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>plative part of his nature which is elaborated in the perfect copy. This great scene,
as it was first written, appeared to the poet to have been scarcely capable of improve-
ment.
<P>The character of Polonius, under the name of Corambis, presents itself in the
original copy with little variation. We have extension, but not change. As we
proceed we find that Shakspere, in the first copy, more emphatically marked the
supposed madness of Hamlet than he thought fit to do in the amended copy. Thus
Ophelia does not, as now, say,&mdash;&lquo;Alas, my lord, my lord, I have been so affrighted,&rquo;
but she comes at once to proclaim Hamlet <I>mad.</I> [See lines 664-672 of Q<SUB>1</SUB>.]
<P>Again, in the next scene, when the King communicates his wishes to Rosencrantz
and Guildenstern, he does not speak of Hamlet as merely put &lquo;from the understand-
ing of himself;&rquo; but in this first copy he says,&mdash;&lquo;Our dear cousin Hamlet Hath lost
the very heart of all his sense.&rquo; In the description which Polonius, in the same
scene, gives of Hamlet's madness for Ophelia's love, the symptoms are made much
stronger in the original copy. [See Q<SUB>1</SUB>, lines 788-792.]
<P>It is curious that, in Burton's <I>Anatomy of Melancholy,</I> we have the stages of
melancholy, madness, and frenzy indicated as described by Celsus; and Burton
himself mentions frenzy as the worst stage of madness, &lquo;clamorous, continual.&rquo; In
the first copy, therefore, Hamlet, according to the description of Polonius, is not
only the prey of melancholy and madness, but by &lquo;continuance&rquo; of frenzy. In the
amended copy the symptoms, according to the same description, are much milder,&mdash;
a sadness&mdash;a fast&mdash;a watch&mdash;a weakness&mdash;a lightness,&mdash;and a madness. The reason
of this change appears to us tolerably clear. Shakspere did not, either in his first
sketch or his amended copy, intend his audience to believe that Hamlet was essen-
tially mad; and he removed, therefore, the strong expressions which might encourage
that belief.
<P>Immediately after the scene of the original copy in which Polonius describes
Hamlet's frenzy, Hamlet comes in and speaks the celebrated soliloquy. In the
amended copy this passage, as well as the scene with Ophelia which follows it, is
placed after Hamlet's interview with the Players. The soliloquy in the first copy is
evidently given with great corruptions, and some of the lines appear transposed by
the printer; on the contrary, the scene with Ophelia is very slightly altered. The
scene with Polonius, now the Second Scene of the Second Act, follows that with
Ophelia in the first copy. In the interview with Guildenstern and Rosencrantz the
dialogue is greatly elaborated in the amended copy; we have the mere germ of the
fine passage, &lquo;This goodly frame,&rquo; &amp;c.&mdash;prose with almost more than the music of
poetry. In the first copy, instead of this noble piece of rhetoric, we have the some-
what tame passage:&mdash;&lquo;Yes, faith, this great world you see contents me not; no, nor
the spangled heavens, nor earth, nor sea; no, nor man, that is so glorious a creature,
contents not me; no, nor woman too, though you laugh.&rquo; . . . .
<P>[Page 90.] Our readers, we think, will be pleased to compare the following pas-
sage of the first copy and the amended play, which offers us an example of the most
surpassing skill in the elaboration of a first idea. [Compare Q<SUB>1</SUB>, lines 1222-1231,
with III, ii, 49-69.]
<P>Schlegel observes that &lquo;Shakspere has composed &ldquo;the play&rdquo; in <I>Hamlet</I> altogether
in sententious rhymes, full of antitheses.&rquo; See the opening speech of the Player
King [III, ii, 145-150]. Here is not only the antithesis, but the artificial elevation,
that was to keep the language of the Interlude apart from that of the real drama.
Shakspere has most skilfully managed the whole business of the Player King and
<PB N=17>
<HE><I>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</I> 17</HE>
<P>Queen upon this principle; but, as we think, when he wrote his first copy, his
power as an artist was not so consummate. In that copy the first lines of the Player
King are singularly flowing and musical; and their sacrifice shows us how inexora-
ble was his judgement. [See Q, lines 1274-1279.]
<P>The soliloquy of the King in the Third Act is greatly elaborated from the first
copy; and so is the scene between Hamlet and his mother. In the Play, as we now
have it, Shakspere has left it doubtful whether the Queen was privy to the murder
of her husband; but in this scene, in the first copy, she says,&mdash;&lquo;But, as I have a soul,
I swear by heaven, I never knew of this most horrid murder.&rquo; And Hamlet, upon
this declaration, says,&mdash;&lquo;And, mother, but assist me in revenge, And in his death
your infamy shall die.&rquo; The Queen, upon this, protests&mdash;&lquo;I will conceal, consent,
and do my best, What stratagem soe'er thou shalt devise.&rquo; In the amended copy the
Queen merely says,&mdash;&lquo;Be thou assured if words be made of breath, And breath of
life, I have no life to breathe What thou hast said to me.&rquo;. . . .
<P>The madness of Ophelia is beautifully elaborated in the amended copy, but all
her snatches of songs are the same in both editions. What she sings, however, in the
First Scene of the original copy is with great art transposed to the Second Scene of
the amended one. The pathos of&mdash;&lquo;And will he not come again?&rquo; is doubled, as it
now stands, by the presence of Laertes.
<P>We are now arrived at a scene in the Quarto of 1603 altogether different from
anything we find in the amended copy. It is a short scene between Horatio and the
Queen, in which Horatio relates Hamlet's return to Denmark, and describes the
treason which the King had plotted against him, as well as the mode by which he
had evaded it by the sacrifice of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. The Queen, with
reference to the &lquo;&mdash;&mdash; subtle treason that the King had plotted,&rquo; says: &lquo;Then I per-
ceive there's treason in his looks,&rquo; &amp;c. [See Q<SUB>1</SUB>, lines 1756-1759.]
<P>This is decisive as to Shakspere's original intentions with regard to the Queen,
but the suppression of the scene in the amended copy is another instance of his ad-
mirable judgement. She does not redeem her guilt by entering into plots against
her guilty husband; and it is far more characteristic of the irregular impulses of
Hamlet's mind, and of his subjection to circumstances, that he should have no con-
fidences with his mother, and form with her and Horatio no plans of revenge. The
story of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern is told in six lines. [See Q<SUB>1</SUB>, 1773-1778.]
The expansion of this simple passage into the exquisite narrative of Hamlet to Ho-
ratio of the same circumstances presents, to our minds, a most remarkable example
of the difference between the mature and the youthful intellect.
<P>The scene of the Grave-digger, in the original copy, has all the great points of the
present scene. The frenzy of Hamlet at the grave is also the same. Who but the
poet himself could have worked up this line&mdash;&lquo;Anon, as mild and gentle as a dove,&rquo;
into&mdash;&lquo;Anon, as patient as the female dove, When that her golden couplets are dis-
closed, His silence will sit drooping.&rquo;? The scene with Osric is greatly expanded in
the amended copy. The catastrophe appears to be the same; but the last leaf of the
copy of 1603 is wanting [<I>sic</I> in Knight's last edition]. . . . .
<P>We must express our decided opinion, grounded upon an attentive comparison of
the original sketch with the perfect play, that the original sketch was an early pro-
duction of our poet. The copy of 1603 is no doubt piratical; it is unquestionably
very imperfectly printed. But if the passage about the &lquo;inhibition&rquo; of the players
fixes the date of the perfect play as 1600, which we believe it does, the essential dif-
ferences between the sketch and the perfect play,&mdash;differences which do not depend
<PB N=18>
<HE>18 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>upon the corruption of a text,&mdash;can only be accounted for upon the belief that there
was a considerable interval between the productions of the first and second copy,
in which the author's power and judgement had become mature, and his peculiar
habits of philosophical thought had been completely established. This is a matter
which does not admit of proof within our limited space, but the passages which
we have already given from the original copy do something to prove it. . . . .
<P>In proof that <I>Romeo and Juliet</I> is one of Shakspere's early plays, Hallam points
out the &lquo;want of that thoughtful philosophy which, when once it had germinated in
Shakspere's mind, never ceased to display itself.&rquo; The <I>Hamlet</I> of 1604 is full of
this &lquo;thoughtfull philosophy.&rquo; But the original sketch, as given in Q<SUB>1</SUB>, exhibits few
traces of it in the form of didactic observations. Note the following passages which
are <I>not there found:</I> &lquo;For nature crescent,&rquo; &amp;c., I, iii, 11; &lquo;This heavy-headed
revel,&rquo; &amp;c., I, iv, 17; &lquo;There is nothing, either good or bad, but thinking makes it
so,&rquo; &amp;c., II, ii, 244; &lquo;I could be bounded in a nutshell,&rquo; &amp;c., II, ii, 249; &lquo;Bring
me to the test,&rquo; &amp;c., III, iv, 142; &lquo;I see a cherub,&rquo; &amp;c., IV, iii, 47; &lquo;Nature is fine
in love,&rquo; &amp;c., IV, v, 157; &lquo;There's a divinity,&rquo; &amp;c., V, ii, 10. Further, the plays
which belong to the beginning of the seventeenth century, as Hallam points out,
indicate a censuring of mankind. If, then, this quality be not found in the original
sketch of <I>Hamlet,</I> we may refer that sketch to an earlier period. It is remarkable
that in this sketch the misanthropy, if so it may be called, of Hamlet can scarcely
be traced; his feelings have altogether reference to his personal griefs and doubts.
The first <I>Hamlet</I> was, we think, written when this &lquo;bitter remembrance,&rquo; whatever
it was, had no place in his heart. Note the following passages, which indicate these
morbid feelings, which are wanting in Q<SUB>1</SUB>: &lquo;How weary, flat, stale, and unprofitable,&rquo;
&amp;c., I, ii, 133; &lquo;Denmark's a prison,&rquo; &amp;c., II, ii, 239; &lquo;I have of late . . . . lost all
my mirth,&rquo; &amp;c., II, ii, 288. The soliloquy, &lquo;To be, or not to be,&rquo; &amp;c., where the
outpourings of a wounded spirit are generalized in the Q<SUB>1</SUB>, III, i, 56; &lquo;Absent thee
from felicity awhile,&rquo; &amp;c., V, ii, 334, 335. These examples are sufficient, we think,
to show that we have internal evidence that the original sketch and the augmented
and perfect copy of <I>Hamlet</I> were written under different influences and habits of
thought.
<P>[The argument against the early composition of <I>Hamlet,</I> derived from the nega-
tive testimony of Francis Meres, who in 1598 mentioned twelve plays of Shake-
speare's, among which <I>Hamlet</I> is not named, Knight (<I>Chronology of Shakespeare's
Plays</I>) opposes by contending that Meres's list is not to be supposed to be complete.
&lquo;The expression which Meres uses, &ldquo;for comedy <I>witness,</I>&rdquo; implies that he selects
particular examples of excellence.&rquo;]
<P>Thus far Knight. No one, I think, can deny that his remarks are shrewd and
forcible.
<P>A writer in <SC>The Edinburgh Review</SC> (April, 1845, vol. lxxxi, p. 378) maintains
the same views, as follows:
<P>The reason of the thing has long made it be admitted as probable that Shake-
speare's activity as an original dramatist must have commenced much sooner than
the dates commonly assigned to the oldest of his works in the received copies. . . . .
In these circumstances we find that a play named <I>Hamlet,</I> and described by marks
tending to establish (though not decisively establishing) its identity with a play of
Shakespeare's is mentioned as existing in 1587, or the poet's twenty-fifth year [<I>sic</I>];
and that similar notices occur in 1594 and 1596. We are thus entitled to assume it
as probable that <I>Hamlet</I> did exist, in one shape or another, from the oldest of those
<PB N=19>
<HE><I>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</I> 19</HE>
<P>dates. If any of us still have difficulty in believing that this drama, as we possess
it in its complete form,&mdash;the most deeply contemplative of all its author's works,&mdash;
could have come into being as an effusion of his earliest manhood, there is now at
hand the hypothesis,&mdash;rendered plausible by what we know in regard to other works
of his,&mdash;that, as first composed, <I>Hamlet</I> may have been not inconsiderably unlike
what it is in the shape best known to us. So far we are entitled to proceed without
knowing that any edition exists which throws more light on the question.
<P>When we open the Quarto of 1603, the conjectures previously formed become
certainties. Though we had otherwise no reason to suspect that <I>Hamlet</I> had existed
in a different shape before its publication in 1604, we should at once perceive that it
had done so; and that the edition of 1603, notwithstanding the imperfections and
blunders which make it perhaps the very worst of all the badly printed plays of the
time, does yet present no unsatisfactory representation of the state and peculiarities
of the work in its earlier form. Afterwards, taking again into account the external
circumstances, we find them to square, as exactly as could be expected, with the
internal evidence afforded by a comparison of the editions. In short, we have no
difficulty in believing that Q<SUB>1</SUB> gives us, although with provoking imperfections and
corruptions, a form of the work older by a good many years than that in which we
have been accustomed to study it,&mdash;a form exhibiting such dissimilarities from the later
one, as indicate not obscurely the progress of the poet's mind, from the unripe fervor
of early manhood to the calmer and more philosophic inspiration of perfect maturity.
<P>[Page 380.] In other words, the older Play evolves but partially either of the ele-
ments of the Prince's contemplative character,&mdash;the philosophic and the poetic,&mdash;those
deep and fine touches of a moody and cheerless yet noble philosophy,&mdash;those daz-
zling flashes of imaginative light which make all that is around them blaze up with
reflected splendor. But it wants more of the philosophy than of the poetry. Al-
though the story, as Knight has appositely observed, does really, when we reflect
upon its accumulation of revolting and bloody incidents, present an aspect which
throws it back into the school of <I>Titus Andronicus;</I> although it is one which, per-
haps, Shakespeare would not in later years have selected, in its full mass of horror
at least, as a fit subject for genuine tragedy; yet, even in the earliest form in which
we possess the drama, we perceive the theme to have been idealized by the high
working of a great poetic mind. Thus, in the First Act, which puts in representa-
tion the most imaginative features of the idea, there is not in the most prominent
parts a material difference between the two editions. The mighty conception had
arisen in the young poet's imagination with full and ripe distinctness; and that rich
strength of words and of illustrative images, that bright array of lights and shades
caught from external nature and reflected back upon the poetic heart, that early ease
and felicity which he had proved in his youthful lyrics and descriptive verses, here
enabled him to bestow on the induction of his drama a development to which subse-
quent changes in his own mind qualified him to add but little. The Ghost scenes
receive only some additional polishing and a few additional strokes of imagery. It
is in the minor scenes,&mdash;the scene at court, and the interview of Corambis (the Po-
lonius of the old play) with his two children,&mdash;that the material changes occur. In
them there is a remodelling of almost everything. Even in the First Act, however,
there are not a few instances which would exemplify well the gradual progress by
which the character of Hamlet reached its full complement of representation. His
first soliloquy, although glaringly misprinted in the older copy, is as apt an illustra-
tion as any.
<PB N=20>
<HE>20 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>In subsequent parts of the play, Shakespeare's views are perceived to have
changed in many most important respects during the interval between the two copies.
Much of this is seen in the elaboration of particular passages, of which specimens
are given by Knight. Much of it will be seen, also, on an intelligent and patient
analysis, in those transpositions which some crities would charge altogether to the
account of the copyists. One of these may be noticed as illustrative of those broader
conceptions of his art,&mdash;of that increase of gentleness and calmness, and of that
addiction to gradual preparation for startling and violent scenes of passion,&mdash;which
were taught to the poet by increased experience in thought and in dramatic com-
position.
<P>A whole scene is transposed; the famous interview with Ophelia, where he madly
reproaches and reviles her,&mdash;a scene whose harshness may not always be perceived
in the closet, but from which, in acting, no skill has been able, unless by a gross vio-
lation of the text and meaning of the author, to remove an impression approaching
to actual pain.
<P>Let us recollect the place which this scene, so unharmonious in its palpable
effect, holds in the drama. Let us recollect, also, how we are prepared for its
approach.
<P>In the play, as we have it in the newer edition, Hamlet's assumed madness is an-
nounced by degrees. First comes Ophelia to describe that pitiful act in which he
had seemed to bid her an everlasting farewell. Then the King talks of Hamlet's
&lquo;transformation,&rquo; and sets the court-sponges to suck out the heart of his secret; and
Polonius reasons wisely, like many other wise men, from false premises. After this,
Hamlet himself enters, reading; and next ensues that most characteristic dialogue
with Polonius, and afterwards with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, in which there
alternate deep scorn, wild and aimless taunting, majestic imagination, and philo-
sophic thought,&mdash;and that unspeakably profound pathos, that hopeless sinking of
the heart, which, recurring with increasing frequency as the drama proceeds, makes
us feel more and more keenly that, after all, the Prince's madness was not wholly
put on,&mdash;that the struggle of his intellect with his will had truly shaken the founda-
tions upon which reason builds her seat. Afterwards come the Players; and when
they have departed, the Prince bursts out into that terrific outbreak of passion, of
self-reproach, of self-contempt, of grief, of hatred, and, finally, of determined re-
venge, which concentrates his whole history, and an abstract of his whole character,
within the compass of less than a hundred lines. Thus, in the altered play, closes
Act Second; and it is only at the opening of the Third that we find the scene with
Ophelia.
<P>But all this was originally managed by the poet in a different manner. The scene
with Ophelia was inserted long before in all its harshness; nay, with an abruptness
bringing it somewhat closer to the scene in the original Novel,&mdash;that coarse and
mean model from which, for this as for much else, so very many things were bor-
rowed. In the sketch the scene comes immediately after the wise reasonings of
Polonius; and, introduced by the soliloquy, &lquo;To be, or not to be,&rquo; it is Hamlet's first
appearance since his interview with his father's spirit. The rough outline of the
fine dialogue with Polonius and the two sponges immediately follows it. This was
what Shakespeare planned when he first wrote the play; we know what he did
when he came to revise it.
<P>The change may be regarded in several lights. It may be thought of as bringing
out the strong scene with Ophelia, after more gradual and complete preparation,&mdash;as
<PB N=21>
<HE><I>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</I> 21</HE>
<P>thus at once softening the seeming sternness of the scene itself, and developing
Hamlet's character, both as it was and as it seemed, with a more effective climax.
Or it may be thought of in a higher view, as an expedient bearing upon the harmo-
nious arrangement of the Play as a whole,&mdash;as enabling the imagination to contem-
plate the dramatic panorama more easily, and the sympathy to flow more quickly and
smoothly with the current of the emotion. It may be thought of as infusing greater
breadth and simplicity, and a stronger degree of contrast, into the masses into which
the drama naturally falls. According to the old arrangement, there was in some
measure a frittering away of strength,&mdash;a dividing of efforts which would have been
better made in unison. The energetic passion of the scene with Ophelia breaks out
suddenly and passes away without effect. The remainder of the Act is in a key far
less passionate. And, again, when we come to the Third Act the vehemence of the
play-scene breaks out with equal unexpectedness. Take the altered shape of the
drama. How differently does everything now proceed! The Second Act is now an
uninterrupted series of scenes, marked by repose; a broad mass of light on the pic-
ture, with heavy shadows on this side and on that. The mind of the Prince, the
minds of all who stand about him, are for a time quiescent, brooding, expectant.
And then, in the Third Act, of which the transposed scene is the opening, comes the
convulsion, shock after shock;&mdash;the wild insults heaped upon Ophelia,&mdash;the sup-
pressed suspicion which begins the play-scene,&mdash;the mad jubilee of revenge and
hate which reigns in its close,&mdash;the vainly remorseful prayer of the murderer, with
Hamlet's fiendish paroxysm of cool malice as he watches him on his knees (one of
the most significant touches in the whole piece),&mdash;and, last of all, the fiery haste
and terrible impressiveness of the scene in the Queen's chamber, which contains the
slaughter of Polonius, the fearfully earnest reproof administered to the guilty mother,
the apparition of the murdered father, awful and portentous.
<P>The most eminent followers of Knight, although differing from him somewhat in
minor details, are <SC>Delius, Elze, Staunton</SC>, and <SC>Dyce</SC>, and their views will be set
forth briefly before the arguments of the other side are given. It is well to remem-
ber the point under discussion: whether, making a full allowance for a certain per-
centage of typographical errors, the differences between Q<SUB>1</SUB> and Q<SUB>2</SUB> are due to a re-
modelling of the play by Shakespeare, or merely to the very imperfect transcript
from which Q<SUB>1</SUB> was printed. <SC>Knight</SC> may be considered as the chiefest advocate of
the former theory, <SC>Collier</SC> the earliest of the latter.
<P><SC>Delius</SC> agrees with Knight in so far as that the variation between Q<SUB>1</SUB> and Q<SUB>2</SUB> is appar-
ently too great to be wholly explained on Collier's hypothesis. After eliminating all
the sources of corruption which Collier enumerates, there still remain differences
between the two texts which can be attributed to the poet and to the poet alone, <I>e. g.</I>
the change of names; the transposition of scenes; rhymed verses which no piratical
printer would or could make; and, finally, the scene between the Queen and Horatio
must have been Shakespeare's work. Knight does not seem to have given due
weight to the corruption which Q<SUB>1</SUB> received at the unskilful hands of the printers.
As Q<SUB>1</SUB> now stands, Shakespeare never wrote it, with all its omissions, abbrevia-
tions, and sophistications. If the old tragedy of which we have traces were not a
youthful production of Shakespeare's, it is very possible that he drew largely from it
for his own tragedy. Robertes was probably hindered from publishing the edition
for which he took out a license by the unwillingness of the actors to permit the pub-
lic to see the Play in any other way than on the stage. But as the interest of the
<PB N=22>
<HE>22 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>public in the Play continued, N. L. and John Trundell started the fraudulent specu-
lation of offering for sale their version of the Play as though it were the same as that
which was holding tbe stage in 1603. [The omission to account for the way in which
N. L. and John Trundell obtained possession of a version while James Robertes could
not, is not to be laid to the desire for condensation on the part of the present <SC>Ed.</SC>] This
imposture, and such impostures were not uncommon in those days, coupled with the
fear lest this spurious version should prove injurious to the acted Play, incited the
actors of Shakespeare's company to put their genuine version in press. The title-
page of Q<SUB>2</SUB> proves that its publication was due to the fraudulent edition of tbe pre-
ceding year. The words: &lquo;<I>enlarged to almost as much againe as it was,</I>&rquo; possibly do
not refer to any remodelling of tbe Play by Shakespeare, but to Q<SUB>1</SUB>, upon which the
object was to throw discredit in all respects, as an unauthorized and defective edition.
But, according to the usage in theatrical matters of those times, such antagonistic
competition among publishers applied only to a <I>new</I> drama; wherefore the version
of <I>Hamlet,</I> as set forth in the Qq, may be safely attributed to the beginning of the
seventeenth century, or about the middle of Shakespeare's productive career.
<P><SC>Elze</SC>, (<I>Einleitung. Hamlet.</I> Leipzig, 1857, p. xix), after quoting the references
by Nash, Henslowe, Lodge, &amp;c., to the old tragedy, says: All these allusions have
been referred to a <I>Hamlet</I> preceding Shakespeare's, because it is universally assumed
that Shakespeare arrived in London in 1586, and did not take the <I>Hamlet</I> in band,
as it then existed, until 1597-1598. And the reason why this date is selected is be-
cause Francis Meres, in his <I>Palladis Tamia</I> of that year, did <I>not</I> enumerate <I>Hamlet</I>
among Shakespeare's other Plays. Now, from the connection in which this passage
occurs, it follows by no manner of means that Meres intended to give a complete
list of all Shakespeare's works that had appeared up to that time, but merely
vouchers sufficient to prove his assertion tbat Shakespeare was the Plautus and
Seneca among Englishmen; Meres mentioned as many comedies as tragedies, just
six of each kind, probably tbose that he held in highest esteem, and whicb would be
the most likely to carry the name of the poet down to posterity. For not only <I>Ham-
let,</I> which assuredly did not exist at that time in the complete shape whicb has inspired
the wonder of succeeding ages, but <I>Pericles</I> also and <I>Henry VI,</I> are lacking in this
list of Meres's Plays, and they were undoubtedly written and bad been acted before
1598. The assumption of the existence of an ante-Sbakespearian <I>Hamlet</I> is a mere
make-shift to which recourse has been had througb inability to reconcile the forego-
ing facts and allusions with Shakespeare's <I>Hamlet</I> as it was subsequently put forth.
<P>[Page xxii.] Tbere are two arguments which have hitherto escaped notice, by
means of which we can approximate to the date of tbe earliest sketch of <I>Hamlet.</I>
First: Shakespeare's ridicule of Euphuism, not only in the character of Osric, but
also of the Grave-digger, who is a Euphuist in his way. In the scene with the
latter Hamlet alludes to the &lquo;three years&rquo; since the &lquo;age has grown so picked.&rquo;
Now Lily's <I>Euphues</I> appeared, according to Malone and Collier, in 1579, accord-
ing to Watts, in 1580, and according to Drake, in 1581; allowing some time for it
to permeate all classes of society, we have the year 1585 as about the time to which
Hamlet may allude. Secondly: in 1585, Shakespeare's son Hamnet was born,
one of twins. This unusual increase to his family must have added greatly to the
distress of Shakespeare's already straitened circumstances; and the youthful father
and poet was driven to London to seek bis fortunes. It is perhaps not too much to
say that it was this little son that forced bim to London. Is it not readily conceiva-
ble that at the very beginning of his career he should have chosen a subject for bis
<PB N=23>
<HE><I>THE DATE, AND THE TEXT</I> 23</HE>
<P>pen which bore the same name as his beloved boy, and that he should have recurred
to it afterwards with undisguised preference? Hamnet died in 1596; and this blow,
which must have fallen most heavily on the father, may possibly have led him to
take up once more this spiritual child of tbe same name. Who can estimate the
effect which grief for his only son may not have had in producing that deep-
seated melancholy and distaste for the vanity of the world which have found in this
tragedy their immortal expression?
<P>[Page xxiv.] Further speculations are idle, as to how often or in what yea<*>
Shakespeare remodelled <I>Hamlet;</I> it suffices to know that in Q<SUB>1</SUB> we have the next to
tbe last version, and in Q<SUB>2</SUB> the last version. It must not be understood that the re-
vision was made between these dates; on the contrary, the allusion to the &lquo;inhibition&rquo;
[see Notes, II, ii, 320] proves that it must have been between 1600 and 1602.
<P><SC>Timmins</SC> (<I>Preface to the Devonshire Hamlets,</I> p. ix): From allusions in literature
at the close of the sixteenth century it is a reasonable assumption that this drama,
bearing date 1603, may have been a recognized work of Shakespeare, publicly per-
formed several years before that date and surreptitiously printed in that year. This
would allow the further inference that tbe subject was a favorite one with Shake-
speare, and that about the beginning of the seventeenth century he revised his early
drama, and &lquo;enlarged it to almost as much againe as it was.&rquo; . . . . My conviction is
that in Q<SUB>1</SUB> we have a &lquo;rougb-hewn&rquo; draft of a noble drama (written probably 1587-
1589), &lquo;diverse times acted by His Highnesse servants&rquo; till 1602, when it was &lquo;en
tered&rquo; for publication, and soon afterwards &lquo;enlarged,&rquo; and &lquo;shaped,&rquo; as it appear
in Q<SUB>2</SUB>, by the divine bard's maturer mind.
<P><SC>Staunton</SC>: What really concerns us is to know whether, making large allowance
for omissions and corruptions due to the negligence of those tbrougb wbose hands
tbe manuscript passed, the edition of 1603 exhibits the play as Shakespeare first
wrote it and as it was &lquo;diverse times acted.&rquo; We believe it does. The internal
evidence is to our judgement convincing that in this wretchedly printed copy we
bave the poet's first conception (written probably at an early stage of his dramatic
career) of that magnificent tragedy which, remodelled and augmented, was published
in 1604.
<P><SC>Dyce</SC> (ed. 2, 1866): It seems certain tbat in Q<SUB>1</SUB> (as is the case with respect to
the earliest Quartos of <I>The Merry Wives of Windsor</I> and <I>Romeo and Juliet</I>) we
bave Sbakespeare's first conception of the Play, tbough with a text mangled and
corrupted throughout, and perhaps formed on the notes of some short-hand writer,
who had imperfectly taken it down during representation. Not to dwell on other
particulars, the names borne by Polonius and Reynaldo in Q<SUB>1</SUB> are alone sufficient to
show that the said Quarto exhibits a form of the tragedy very different from that
which it afterwards assumed in Q<SUB>2</SUB> and F<SUB>1</SUB>.
<P>The following remarks of <SC>Hunter's</SC> belong to this side of the question, but are

<P><SC>Hunter</SC> (<I>New Illust.,</I> &amp;c., ii, 204): The exact mode of the preparation of this
tragedy will probably never be fully ascertained. Shakespeare seems to have worked
upon it in a manner different from what was bis usual practice. We collect from
the newly-discovered copy, not only that large additions were made to the play after
it had been presented at the theatres, but that very material changes were made in
the distribution of the scenes and the order of events. This seems to show that
there was no period when the poet sat down to bis work having a settled project in
<PB N=24>
<HE>24 <I>APPENDIX</I></HE>
<P>his mind, and meaning to work out tbe design continuously from the opening to the
catastrophe; and this may be, after all, the true reason of the difficulty, which has
always been felt, of determining wbat the character really is in which the poet
meant to invest the hero of the piece. It may account, also, for the introduction of
scenes which appear to have been written for the sake of themselves alone; beau-
tiful in themselves, but neither necessary for the maintenance of a general harmony
in the whole, nor for carrying on the business of the story. To this want of con-
tinuity in the composition of the piece, and of having the mind steadily intent on
one design, plan, and object, is also to be attributed the great falling off in the later
portions, and the lame and impotent manner in which what ought to be the grand
catastrophe is at last brought about.
<P>It sbould perhaps be noticed that <SC>Gervinus</SC> follows Knight.
<P>Thus far the advocates of the theory that in Q<SUB>1</SUB> we have a reproduction, imperfect
and garbled it is true, of the old <I>Hamlet,</I> alluded to by Nash and others, and written
by Shakespeare in his youth, and revised by him in his maturer years.
<P>On the other band it is contended that Q<SUB>1</SUB> and Q<SUB>2</SUB> represent the same version, the
difference between the two editions indicating not the growth of Shakespeare's
mind, but the carelessness or incompetence of short-hand writers, transcribers, and
printers.
<P><SC>Collier</SC>, as has been before stated, believes that Q<SUB>1</SUB> was put forth by some name-
less and unscrupulous printer from an imperfect manuscript of a play surreptitiously
obtained, and that but few copies were sold, as its worthlessness was soon discovered.
As accurate reprints of this Quarto are accessible, Collier says: &lquo;it will be unneces-
sary to go in detail into proofs to establish, as we could do without much difficulty,
tbe following points:
<P>&lquo;1. That great part of the play, as it there stands, was taken down in short-hand.
<P>&lquo;2. That where mechanical skill failed the short-hand writer, he eitber filled up the
blanks badly from memory, or employed an inferior writer to assist him.
<P>&lquo;3. That although some of the scenes were carelessly transposed, and others en-
tirely omitted, in the edition of 1603, the drama, as it was acted while the short-hand
writer was employed in taking it down, was, in all its main features, the same as the
more perfect copy of the tragedy printed with the date of 1604. It is true that in
the edition of 1603, Polonius is called Corambis, and his servant Montano, and we
may not be able to determine why these cbanges were made in the immediately sub-
sequent impression; but we may, perhaps, conjecture that they were names in the
older play on the same story, or names which Shakespeare at first introduced and
subsequently thought fit to reject. We know that Ben Jonson changed the whole
<I>dramatis person&aelig;</I> of his <I>Every Man in his Humour.</I> [<SC>Dyce</SC>, after quoting this
last sentence, adds: &lquo;Perhaps they were names which Shakespeare had originally
retained from tbe earlier drama, and which, on revising and altering his tragedy, he
changed to Polonius and Reynaldo.&rquo;]
<P>&lquo;But although we entirely reject Q<SUB>1</SUB> as an authentic <I>Hamlet,</I> it is of bigh value in
enabling us to settle the text of various important passages. It proves, besides, that
certain portions of the play as it appears in F<SUB>1</SUB>, which do not form part of Q<SUB>2</SUB>, were
originally acted, and were not, as has been hitherto imagined, subsequent intro-
ductions.&rquo;
<P><SC>W. W. Lloyd</SC> (<I>Critical Essay on Hamlet,</I> contributed to <SC>Singer's</SC> Second Edi-
tion, p. 345): I confess that the <I>Hamlet</I> of Q<SUB>1</SUB>, marred and mangled as it is, does

<P>not give me the impression of one of Shakespeare's early works, and if some early
